title: The Passion Narrative: The Story of Jesus’ Crucifixion and Resurrection
subtitle: The Gospel accounts, the Christian confession, and the Quranic account
summary: The Passion Narrative is the New Testament account of Jesus’ final meal, arrest, trial, crucifixion, burial, and reported resurrection. Christianity treats these events as central to salvation. Islam honors Jesus as the Messiah but teaches that his enemies neither killed nor crucified him, and that Allah raised him. The difference concerns the meaning of Jesus’ mission as well as the historical account.

seo.metaTitle: The Passion Narrative: Crucifixion and Resurrection | The Straight Path
seo.metaDescription: A concise comparison of the Gospel Passion Narrative, the Christian confession of resurrection, and the Quranic account of Jesus.

sections.title: Understanding the Passion Narrative
sections.body:
The Passion Narrative is the name commonly given to the final part of the Gospel story: Jesus’ last meal with his disciples, his arrest, hearings before Jewish and Roman authorities, crucifixion, burial, and the discovery of the empty tomb. The four Gospels tell the same broad story with different selections of detail and emphasis.

For Christians, the narrative is not simply a record of a martyr’s death. It is the center of the Christian confession that Jesus died for sins and was raised. For Muslims, Jesus is the honored Messiah and a great messenger, but the Quran rejects the claim that his enemies killed or crucified him and states that Allah raised him.

sections.title: The Christian Story in the New Testament
sections.body:
Matthew 26–28, Mark 14–16, Luke 22–24, and John 18–20 narrate Jesus’ final days. They agree on the central sequence: a final meal, arrest, trial, crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, burial, an empty tomb, and appearances reported by Jesus’ followers. The accounts differ in some chronology and detail, but each presents the crucifixion and resurrection as decisive events.

Paul’s summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 is especially important because it is earlier than the written Gospels. It states that Christ died for sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to named followers and others. Christian theology reads this as the heart of the apostolic proclamation.

sections.title: Where the Gospel Accounts Differ
sections.body:
The Gospels are four narratives, not four identical transcripts. They vary in the names and actions emphasized at the tomb, the wording of sayings from the cross, the timing of particular scenes, and the order in which appearances are described. Christian interpreters commonly explain these differences as selective reporting, compression, and complementary perspectives. Historical-critical scholars often see evidence of distinct literary purposes and sources.

These differences do not remove the shared Christian claim. Each Gospel presents Jesus’ death and the proclamation of his resurrection as central. The question is whether the accounts can be harmonized in detail and, more fundamentally, whether the events should be understood through the Christian or Quranic account of Jesus.

sections.title: Why the Resurrection Is Central to Christianity
sections.body:
Christianity understands the crucifixion as an atoning death and the resurrection as God’s vindication of Jesus. The New Testament connects these claims to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and hope beyond death. Without the resurrection, Paul says, Christian preaching and faith would be empty.

Muslims should represent this conviction accurately. The disagreement is not over whether Christians take the events seriously, but over whether the crucifixion occurred and whether Jesus should be understood as a divine savior.

sections.title: The Quranic Account of Jesus
sections.body:
The Quran honors Jesus as the Messiah, son of Mary, and messenger of Allah. It rejects the boast that his opponents killed him: Quran 4:157 states that they did not kill him or crucify him, while Quran 4:158 states that Allah raised him to Himself.

The Quran does not name another person who was crucified in Jesus’ place. Classical Muslim commentators offered more than one explanation of the phrase that the event was made to appear so, including substitution accounts and readings centered on confusion or appearance. The core Islamic belief is the Quran’s clear denial that Jesus was killed by his enemies and its affirmation that Allah saved and raised him.

sections.title: The Central Difference
sections.body:
The Passion Narrative brings a central difference between Christianity and Islam into focus. Christianity sees the crucifixion and resurrection as the saving climax of Jesus’ divine mission. Islam sees Jesus as a human messenger whom Allah protected, and rejects the idea that salvation requires the death of a divine son.

The disagreement cannot be reduced to a minor chronological question. It concerns revelation, the nature of God, the identity of Jesus, and how God forgives. Both accounts should be considered from their own primary texts before their claims are compared.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: The Passion Narrative
sections.body:
The Gospel accounts share a Passion Narrative in which Jesus is crucified, buried, and proclaimed risen. Their individual details are not identical, and the relationship between the accounts remains a subject of Christian interpretation and historical study.

The Quran gives a different account: Jesus’ enemies did not kill or crucify him, and Allah raised him. This places the Islamic and Christian understandings of Jesus at a decisive point of disagreement while preserving Islam’s deep honor for Jesus and Mary.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do the four Gospels tell one identical Passion Narrative?
A: No. They share the central story but differ in literary arrangement and individual details. Christians commonly read the accounts as complementary; historical-critical scholars often analyze the differences as evidence of each author’s distinctive sources and aims.

Q: Does Islam deny Jesus?
A: No. Belief in Jesus as the Messiah and a messenger of Allah is required in Islam. The Quran affirms his virgin birth and miracles by Allah’s permission while rejecting his divinity and crucifixion.

Q: Does the Quran identify someone else who was crucified?
A: No. Quran 4:157 does not name a substitute. Muslim commentators have differed about the details, but the verse’s central claim is that Jesus was not killed or crucified by his enemies.

Q: Why does this disagreement matter?
A: The crucifixion and resurrection are central to Christian salvation theology, while Islam’s account safeguards the absolute oneness of God and Jesus’ status as His honored messenger.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
- **The Crucifixion and the Qur’an: A Study in the History of Muslim Thought** — Todd Lawson. A scholarly study of Muslim interpretations of Quran 4:157.
- **The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach** — Michael R. Licona. A detailed Christian historical defense of the resurrection.
- **The Historical Figure of Jesus** — E. P. Sanders. A widely used introduction to historical study of Jesus and the early Christian movement.

quranVerses.arabic: وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا ٱلْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱخْتَلَفُوا۟ فِيهِ لَفِى شَكٍّۢ مِّنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِۦ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا ٱتِّبَاعَ ٱلظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًۢا
quranVerses.translation: And [for] their saying, ‘Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.’ And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain.

bibleVerses.text: For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
